title: Rosalyn Yalow and the Radioimmunoassay

trailer.text: Rosalyn Yalow (1921–2011) was an American medical physicist, and on October 13, 1977, she learned that she had won the Nobel Prize.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, she was born into a Jewish family in the Bronx, New York, and received a doctorate in physics.
In 1950 she was appointed physicist in the radioisotope service of a Veterans Administration hospital, and there she found a research partner, the young doctor Solomon Berson.
Together they used radioactive isotopes to study what happens inside the human body, and she received the Nobel Prize "for the development of radioimmunoassays of peptide hormones".
According to an estimate cited in her Nobel lecture, in 1975 more than 4000 clinical laboratories in the United States alone performed tests using this method.

stations.title: A girl from New York who wanted to be a teacher

paragraphs.text: Rosalyn Yalow was born on July 19, 1921, in New York.
Her birth name was Rosalyn Sussman.
Her mother was an immigrant and her father came from New York's Lower East Side, and they wanted her to have the education that had been denied them.
She planned to become a teacher.
At 17 she read a biography of Marie Curie and found in her a role model.
In 1939 she heard a lecture by Enrico Fermi on nuclear fission, and the lecture strengthened her determination to devote herself to nuclear science.

stations.title: "She is from New York. She is Jewish. She is a woman."

paragraphs.text: In 1941 Yalow graduated from Hunter College.
After her studies, one university after another turned down her application for advanced studies.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, one admissions office admitted that it believed that, as a Jew and a woman, she would not find a job in the field.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, one admissions officer explained the real reason no graduate program accepted her: "She is from New York. She is Jewish. She is a woman."
Yalow accepted a secretarial job at Columbia University and prepared to take night classes.
At the end of the summer, just before she began working, an offer arrived from the University of Illinois at Urbana.
There Yalow, twenty years old, was the only woman among 400 faculty members and teaching assistants, and one of only three Jews.
During those years she married Aaron Yalow.
In 1945 the two received their doctorates in physics together.

stations.title: A laboratory in a janitor's closet

paragraphs.text: In 1947 the Veterans Administration (VA) hospitals launched a research program on the use of radioactive substances for the diagnosis and treatment of disease.
In 1950 Yalow was appointed physicist and assistant chief of the hospital's radioisotope service, and left teaching.

According to Encyclopedia.com, when she began working in the radioisotope service at the veterans' hospital in the Bronx, in a snowstorm in December, Yalow was given as a small office a converted service room in the hospital wing, and there she set up one of the first radioisotope laboratories in America.
Yalow looked for a research partner with medical experience, and found Solomon Berson, a young doctor at the VA hospital.
In her Nobel lecture she said that from 1950 until his death in 1972, Berson was her partner in the scientific adventure.
For 22 years the two worked together, using radioactive isotopes to study what happens inside the human body.

stations.title: The insulin that disappeared too slowly

paragraphs.text: According to the Nobel lecture, Dr. Arthur Mirsky had hypothesized that maturity-onset diabetes might not be due to a deficiency of insulin secretion, but rather to an abnormally rapid breakdown of insulin by the liver's insulinase.
To test the hypothesis, Yalow and Berson gave diabetic and non-diabetic subjects 131I-labeled insulin intravenously, and followed its metabolism.
They observed that in patients who had already received insulin, the radioactive insulin disappeared from the plasma more slowly.
According to Britannica, they theorized that foreign insulin caused the body to produce antibodies.
According to the Nobel Prize website, it was previously thought that type 2 diabetes was caused by a lack of insulin.
According to the same website, Yalow and Berson proved that it is caused by the body's inefficient use of insulin.
Yalow said that the original paper was rejected by Science, and initially also by the Journal of Clinical Investigation.
According to Encyclopedia.com, most scientists at the time believed that insulin molecules were too small to cause the production of antibodies.
Yalow recounted that the paper was accepted only after a compromise with the editors, in which the words insulin antibody were omitted from the title.
According to Encyclopedia.com, the paper was published in February 1956 in the Journal of Clinical Investigation.
Yalow said that in 1959 the measurement of insulin in human plasma was achieved.
According to the Embryo Project Encyclopedia, before this method, measurements required large blood samples, sometimes too large to be collected.
According to the Embryo Project Encyclopedia, with the development of RIA, researchers could use a single drop of blood to detect and measure the concentration of some biochemical substances.
Yalow described the method's sensitivity: gastrin can be measured at 0.1 picograms per milliliter.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Yalow and Berson said the method was sensitive enough to detect a sugar cube dissolved in Lake Erie, and they toured the United States to promote it.
Yalow said that the first presentation of hormone measurements by the method went virtually unnoticed.
According to her, before 1965 only a few papers from other laboratories appeared in American journals of endocrinology and diabetes.
According to an estimate cited in the Nobel lecture, by 1975 more than 4000 clinical laboratories in the United States alone were performing tests using the method.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, the method was used in thousands of laboratories in the United States and abroad.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, RIA was used for early diagnosis of babies with underactive thyroid glands, thus preventing intellectual disabilities.
Yalow noted that RIA of hepatitis antigen had become the method of choice for testing for infected blood in blood banks in the United States.
According to Encyclopedia.com, thanks to her research American blood banks were cleared of hepatitis-infected plasma.
According to Britannica, the method also made it possible to determine effective dosages of drugs and antibiotics.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Yalow and Berson did not seek to patent the method.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, had Yalow done so she would have become rich, but she did not regret it.
According to Physics Today, RIA has been largely replaced by fluorescent techniques, but immunoassay is still used in routine blood tests.
In 1976, at age 55, Yalow won the Lasker Prize for Basic Medical Research.
According to Physics Today, many considered the Lasker Prize a precursor to the Nobel Prize.
According to Encyclopedia.com, her chances of winning the Nobel were considered slim, and even members of the Nobel committee derided them.
On October 13, 1977, Yalow learned that she had won the Nobel Prize.
The prize citation was "for the development of radioimmunoassays of peptide hormones".
She shared the prize with two other scientists, Andrew Schally and Roger Guillemin, who were honored for their work on hormone production in the brain.
Berson did not receive the prize, because Nobel Prizes are given only to the living, and he died in 1972.
In her Nobel lecture Yalow said of him that she wished he were here to share the moment.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, Yalow was the second woman in the United States to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

According to the Jewish Women's Archive, when she received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in December 1977, Yalow became the first American-born and American-trained woman to receive a Nobel Prize in science.
The archive also notes that she was the first American Jewish woman born in the United States to receive a Nobel Prize.
In her acceptance speech Yalow thanked her mentors, among them Dr. Failla.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, at the ceremonies she spoke about her achievements as a woman.
In 1988 Yalow received the National Medal of Science.
From 1969 Yalow was director of the laboratory, and after Berson's death she named it after him.
She worked sixty to eighty hours a week.
According to the Jewish Women's Archive, under VA policy women had to leave work after five months of pregnancy, but Yalow ignored it.
Her elder child, her son Benjamin, was born in 1952.
Her daughter, Elanna, was born in 1954, and then too Yalow did as she had done after the birth of her son: she returned to the laboratory together with the baby.
According to Physics Today, Yalow did not classify herself as a feminist, but many women scientists saw her as a role model.
According to Encyclopedia.com, she criticized affirmative action and refused the Ladies' Home Journal "Woman of the Year" award.
According to Encyclopedia.com, Yalow said that she never let discriminatory behavior toward her as a Jewish woman control her.
According to the Illinois website, she told students that new ideas are rejected at first, and if they are right, they later become dogma.
Yalow died on May 30, 2011, at the age of 89.
In 2015 a charter school named after her opened in the Bronx.

claims.text: לפי פיזיקס טודיי, פרס לסקר נחשב בעיני רבים מבשר לפרס נובל.
claims.quote: In 1976 Rosalyn was presented with the Albert Lasker Basic Medical Research Award, considered by many to be a precursor to the Nobel Prize.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, סיכוייה של ילו לזכות בנובל נחשבו קלושים ואפילו חברי ועדת נובל זלזלו בהם.
claims.quote: her chances were considered slim; even members of the Nobel committee derided her chances

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה בריטניקה, ילו הייתה מקבלת משותפת של פרס נובל לפיזיולוגיה או רפואה לשנת 1977, יחד עם אנדרו שאלי ורוג'ר גילמן.
claims.quote: joint recipient (with Andrew V. Schally and Roger Guillemin) of the 1977 Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine

claims.text: ילו חלקה את הפרס עם שני מדענים אחרים שהוכרו על עבודתם בייצור הורמונים במוח.
claims.quote: She shared it with two other scientists, who were honored for their work on hormone production in the brain.

claims.text: ברסון לא קיבל את הפרס כי פרסי נובל ניתנים רק לחיים, והוא מת ב-1972.
claims.quote: Since Nobel Prizes are only given to the living, Yalow received the award without Berson, who died in 1972.

claims.text: בהרצאת נובל ילו אמרה על ברסון שהלוואי שהיה כאן לחלוק את הרגע.
claims.quote: Would that he were here to share this moment.

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, ילו הייתה האישה השנייה בארצות הברית שזכתה בנובל לפיזיולוגיה או רפואה.
claims.quote: Rosalyn Yalow was the second woman in the United States to win a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, ב-8 בדצמבר 1977 הפכה ילו לאישה האמריקאית הראשונה, יליד ארצות הברית ובעלת השכלה אמריקאית, שקיבלה פרס נובל במדע.
claims.quote: On December 8, 1977, Rosalyn Yalow became the first American-born and American-trained woman to receive a Nobel Prize in science

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, ילו הייתה האישה היהודייה האמריקאית הראשונה שנולדה בארצות הברית וקיבלה פרס נובל.
claims.quote: and the first American-born Jewish woman to receive a Nobel Prize

claims.text: בנאום הקבלה זיכתה ילו את מנטוריה, כולל ד"ר פאילה.
claims.quote: Yalow credited her mentors, including Dr. Failla, in her acceptance speech

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, ילו התייחסה להישגיה כאישה בטקסי הצגת פרס נובל באוסלו, נורווגיה.
claims.quote: At the Nobel Prize presentation ceremonies in Oslo, Norway, Rosalyn Yalow commented on her achievements as a woman

claims.text: לאחר מות ברסון ילו קראה למעבדה בשמו, והיא הייתה מנהלת המעבדה מ-1969.
claims.quote: she decided eventually to christen her radioimmunoassay facility, of which she had become director in 1969, the Solomon A. Berson Research Laboratory

claims.text: ילו שמרה על לוח עבודה של שישים עד שמונים שעות בשבוע.
claims.quote: She routinely maintained a work schedule of sixty to eighty hours per week.

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, מדיניות ה-VA חייבה נשים לעזוב לאחר חמישה חודשי היריון, אך ילו התעלמה ממנה.
claims.quote: According to policy at the VA, women had to leave once they were five months pregnant, but Yalow ignored it.

claims.text: בנה הבכור של ילו, בנימין, נולד ב-1952.
claims.quote: Rosalyn and Aaron Yalow had their first child, a son, Benjamin, born in 1952.

claims.text: בתה אלנה נולדה ב-1954 וילו פעלה באותו אופן.
claims.quote: When she gave birth to her daughter, Elanna, in 1954, she followed the same procedure.

claims.text: לפי פיזיקס טודיי, ילו לא הגדירה את עצמה פמיניסטית, אך נשים מדענים רבות ראו בה מופת.
claims.quote: Although Rosalyn would never classify herself as a feminist, many women scientists saw her as a role model, just as she viewed Marie Curie.

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ילו ביקרה אפליה מתקנת וסירבה לפרס אשת השנה של Ladies' Home Journal.
claims.quote: she criticized reverse discrimination, and refused the Woman of the Year award of Ladies' Home Journal because she thought men and women should compete on equal terms

claims.text: לפי אנציקלופדיה.קום, ילו אמרה שמעולם לא נתנה להתנהגות מפלה כלפיה כיהודייה לשלוט בה.
claims.quote: Asked if she ever felt stifled by the discrimination against her as a Jewish woman, she responded that she never let such behavior control her.

claims.text: לפי אתר אילינוי, ילו אמרה לתלמידים שרעיונות חדשים נדחים בתחילה ומאוחר יותר הופכים לדוגמה אם צודקים.
claims.quote: Initially, new ideas are rejected. Later they become dogma, if you're right.

claims.text: ילו נפטרה ב-30 במאי 2011 בגיל 89.
claims.quote: She continued to respond to mail from students and give brief interviews until she died on May 30, 2011, at the age of 89.

claims.text: בית ספר צ'רטר נפתח בברונקס ב-2015 ונקרא על שמה של ילו, אחרי מותה.
claims.quote: A few years after Yalow died, in 2015, a K-5 grade charter school opened in the Bronx where she grew up and was named in her honor.

claims.text: רוזלין ילו (1921–2011) הייתה פיזיקאית רפואית אמריקאית, וב-13 באוקטובר 1977 נודע לה על זכייתה בפרס נובל.
claims.quote: Dr. Yalow at the Bronx Veterans Administration Hospital, Oct. 13, 1977

claims.text: לפי ארכיון הנשים היהודיות, כשקיבלה בדצמבר 1977 את פרס הנובל לפיזיולוגיה או רפואה, הפכה ילו לאישה הראשונה ילידת ארצות הברית ובעלת הכשרה אמריקאית שקיבלה פרס נובל במדע.

claims.text: אמה הייתה מהגרת ואביה בא מהלואר איסט סייד שבניו יורק, והם רצו שתקבל את ההשכלה שנמנעה מהם.
